extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, patent practitioners, stakeholders in biotech, diagnostics, and computer-related technologies
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for assessing whether inventions (especially diagnostics, gene-based technologies, and computer-related inventions) meet U.S. patent-eligibility law under current jurisprudence and policy considerations. Emphasizes doctrinal tests, international comparisons, and impacts on innovation, access, and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo–Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court’s two-step framework (commonly called Mayo/Alice) is the controlling test for patent-eligible subject matter: first determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea), then determine whether the claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' or are 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders widely criticized the framework as unworkable and unpredictable. The report notes the framework is applied unevenly by courts and examiners and is central to disputes over eligibility across technologies. Many comments describe the framework as causing uncertainty that harms innovation and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and clarity of 'abstract idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claimed invention is an 'abstract idea' is a threshold inquiry under step one of the Mayo/Alice framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters observe there is no uniform definition of 'abstract idea,' creating subjectivity and unpredictability. Quoted criticisms: 'the “abstract idea” has created havoc' and courts/practitioners lack sufficient guidance to determine the scope of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Significantly more' / 'inventive concept' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under step two of the framework, the claim must recite elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea or otherwise provide an 'inventive concept' to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders say the inquiry is ambiguous and often conflated with novelty/obviousness/enablement (35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112). Examples and commentary question how 'significant' is quantified; commenters give examples where substantial practical improvements were still found ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic claims often required to be linked to treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Current §101 jurisprudence generally requires that claims to diagnostic tests be linked to affirmative steps reciting methods of treatment in order to overcome eligibility rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is criticized as counterintuitive because diagnostic innovators often do not provide treatment; linking to treatment dilutes IP value and raises divided infringement issues. Practically, drafters may need to add treatment-related steps to survive eligibility analysis, with adverse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional standards for diagnostic method eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Different countries treat diagnostic-method patent eligibility differently (examples: China, Korea, Japan, European Patent Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarized stakeholder characterizations: China—diagnostic methods patent eligible so long as method does not lead to diagnosis/health assessment; Korea—diagnosis patentable where claims don’t require the human body to carry out the invention; Japan—may be eligible if performed outside the body or used to collect information; EPO—will not grant patents for diagnostic methods practiced on the human/animal body, but known substances may be patented for use in diagnostics if novel/inventive in that use. Stakeholders use these comparisons to argue for or against U.S. approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility of isolated genes / gene sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether isolated gene sequences (and other gene-based inventions) are patent-eligible subject matter (debate over exclusion of isolated genes as 'natural phenomena').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some associations argue isolated genes when removed from genome have different functioning and merit patent protection (reward disclosure); others argue gene patents hinder research, access, and competition. Stakeholders cite Myriad decision effects—some report increased competition and reduced costs post-Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of patent protection to recoup life-sciences R&D investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy consideration that patents are relied upon by biopharma to recoup substantial R&D costs (examples cited: ~$2.6 billion and ~12 years to bring a drug to market).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry stakeholders use this as a criterion to argue for broader eligibility to preserve incentives for costly, risky drug and diagnostic development. Opposing stakeholders weigh this against concerns about access and competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on access, affordability, and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether extending or restricting patent eligibility will affect public health outcomes, affordability of diagnostics and therapeutics, and competitive markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patient advocacy and public-interest stakeholders argue that restricting eligibility preserves access and competition (citing COVID diagnostics and lower BRCA test costs after Myriad). Industry stakeholders argue restrictions curtail incentives and innovation. The balance of these impacts is presented as a key evaluative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-solution-to-technical-problem (technical character) approach
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative evaluative approach (common in other jurisdictions) that finds claims patentable if they provide a technical solution to a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters recommend focusing on whether the claimed invention provides a technical improvement (easier to apply and more predictable than 'abstract idea' tests). Stakeholders say properly claimed technical solutions are patentable internationally and could align U.S. practice with other offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer-implemented inventions and software
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that computing, algorithms, and software are inherently abstract and pose challenges under the Mayo/Alice framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders argue the test biases against computer-related inventions and dissolves the boundary between claims to algorithms and legitimate system claims that use algorithms. Recommended drafting/claiming strategies include emphasizing improvements in computer technology or detailed technological solutions to problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that claims show an improvement in computer technology
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, computer-implemented inventions should claim an improvement in computer technology or recite a technical solution to a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several companies report success overcoming eligibility rejections by 'going into depth on the technological problem we are addressing and our technological solution.' This approach may also help define the 'abstract idea' and align U.S. practice internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and clarity in USPTO and court application
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether courts and USPTO examiners apply eligibility standards consistently and with adequate technical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters reported inconsistent examiner treatment, over-generalization of components, and failure to appreciate complexity of computer or biotech inventions. Inconsistencies lead to narrow claim scope or added irrelevant limitations solely to satisfy eligibility tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on investment and innovation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of empirical indicators (patent filings, R&D investment, venture capital flows, GDP effects) to assess whether eligibility jurisprudence promotes or harms innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders submitted conflicting data: some report declines in filings and investment linked to uncertainty; others show continued growth in AI/quantum investments. Commenters use such metrics to support competing policy positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific concerns for AI, machine learning, and quantum computing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the current eligibility law adequately protects inventions in transformative computing fields and whether uncertainty reduces U.S. competitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many industry stakeholders warn that uncertainty harms investment and leadership; some argue AI/software should not be made more patentable than other software and even advocate exclusion. The report notes a range of views and the need for careful evaluation by USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of divided infringement when drafting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking diagnostic claims to treatment can implicate divided infringement issues because different parties may perform separate claim steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware that adding affirmative treatment steps to satisfy eligibility can create enforcement difficulties. Commenters note that this dilutes the value of IP for companies that develop diagnostics but do not provide treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: International harmonization as a policy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether adopting approaches consistent with other major jurisdictions would bring predictability to U.S. patent practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple stakeholders recommend considering foreign practices (e.g., technical character test) to reduce uncertainty and align U.S. outcomes with global patent offices. The report contrasts U.S. exclusions with broader protection in some other countries.
